In [[mathematics]], the method of '''clearing denominators''', also called '''clearing fractions''', is a technique for simplifying an [[equation]] equating two expressions that each are a sum of [[Rational function|rational expression]]s – which includes simple [[fraction (mathematics)|fraction]]s.

== Example ==

Consider the equation

: <math> \frac x 6 + \frac y {15z} = 1.</math>

The [[least common multiple|smallest common multiple]] of the two denominators 6 and 15''z'' is 30''z'', so one multiplies both sides by 30''z'':

: <math> 5xz + 2y = 30z. \, </math>

The result is an equation with no fractions.

The simplified equation is not entirely equivalent to the original. For when we substitute {{nowrap|1=''y'' = 0}} and {{nowrap|1=''z'' = 0}} in the last equation, both sides simplify to 0, so we get {{nowrap|1=0 = 0}}, a mathematical truth. But the same substitution applied to the original equation results in {{nowrap|1=''x''/6 + 0/0 = 1}}, which is [[zero divided by zero|mathematically meaningless]].

== Description ==
[[Without loss of generality]], we may assume that the [[right-hand side]] of the equation is 0, since an equation {{nowrap|1={{mvar|E}}<sub>1</sub> = {{mvar|E}}<sub>2</sub>}} may equivalently be rewritten in the form {{nowrap|1={{mvar|E}}<sub>1</sub> − {{mvar|E}}<sub>2</sub> = 0}}.

So let the equation have the form
:<math>\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{P_i}{Q_i} = 0.</math>

The first step is to determine a common denominator {{mvar|D}} of these fractions – preferably the [[least common denominator]], which is the [[least common multiple]] of the {{mvar|Q<sub>i</sub>}}.

This means that each {{mvar|Q<sub>i</sub>}} is a [[Multiplication|factor]] of {{mvar|D}}, so {{nowrap|1={{mvar|D}} = {{mvar|R<sub>i</sub>Q<sub>i</sub>}}}} for some expression {{mvar|R<sub>i</sub>}} that is not a fraction. Then

: <math>\frac{P_i}{Q_i} = \frac{R_i P_i}{R_i Q_i} = \frac{R_i P_i} D \,,</math>

provided that {{mvar|R<sub>i</sub>Q<sub>i</sub>}} does not assume the value 0 – in which case also {{mvar|D}} equals 0.

So we have now

: <math>\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{P_i}{Q_i} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{R_i P_i} D = \frac 1 D \sum_{i=1}^n R_i P_i = 0.</math>

Provided that {{mvar|D}} does not assume the value 0, the latter equation is equivalent with

: <math>\sum_{i=1}^n R_i P_i = 0\,,</math>

in which the denominators have vanished.

As shown by the provisos, care has to be taken not to introduce [[Zero of a function|zero]]s of {{mvar|D}} – viewed as a function of the [[unknown (mathematics)|unknown]]s of the equation – as [[spurious solution]]s.

==Example 2==

Consider the equation

:<math>\frac{1}{x(x+1)}+\frac{1}{x(x+2)}-\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)} = 0.</math>

The least common denominator is {{nowrap|{{mvar|x}}({{mvar|x}} + 1)({{mvar|x}} + 2)}}.

Following the method as described above results in

:<math>(x+2)+(x+1)-x = 0.</math>

Simplifying this further gives us the solution {{nowrap|1={{mvar|x}} = −3}}.

It is easily checked that none of the zeros of {{nowrap|{{mvar|x}}({{mvar|x}} + 1)({{mvar|x}} + 2)}} – namely {{nowrap|1= {{mvar|x}} = 0}}, {{nowrap|1= {{mvar|x}} = −1}}, and {{nowrap|1= {{mvar|x}} = −2}} – is a solution of the final equation, so no spurious solutions were introduced.
